summary: Extends the RFC 3339 timestamp format so a timestamp can carry additional information, including a time zone. It also updates RFC 3339 on how to read the local offset "Z", which no longer implies that UTC is the preferred reference point for the time.

eli5.summary: A time stamp usually says only when something happened. This lets it also say where in the world's time zones it was written down.

questions: what does z mean in a timestamp
subtitle: An optional bracketed suffix lets an RFC 3339 timestamp carry a time zone name and other extra information.

tldr.problem: RFC 3339 timestamps carry very little extra information, so applications that need a time zone name or a calendar choice attach it in non-standard ways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9557 defines the Internet Extended Date/Time Format (IXDTF): an RFC 3339 timestamp followed by optional bracketed tags such as [Europe/Paris] or [u-ca=hebrew]. It also redefines the offset Z as meaning the UTC time is known but the local offset is not.
tldr.outcome: Existing RFC 3339 timestamps stay valid, tags are elective unless marked critical with an exclamation mark, and the RFC updates RFC 3339 on the meaning of Z.

today: RFC 9557 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 3339. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Timestamps Need Extra Information
sections.content:
RFC 3339 defines the Internet timestamp format, which was based on an earlier version of ISO 8601. It lets a timestamp say very little beyond the instant itself. Any other context has to be handled separately or attached in a non-standard way.

This is a problem for applications that keep a time zone name with each instant so that they can account for events such as daylight saving time transitions. Many attach the zone in a non-standard format, at least one of which is fairly well adopted (the RFC points to the Java ZonedDateTime format). Applications might also want to attach more, such as the calendar system in which a time should be shown.

RFC 9557 extends the RFC 3339 format with an optional suffix. The extension is completely optional, so existing RFC 3339 timestamps remain compatible. It is compatible with the popular time-zone-name syntax and gives a general way to attach more information. The RFC calls the result the Internet Extended Date/Time Format (IXDTF).

The scope is deliberately limited to fixed timestamps tied to UTC. Future local times that shift when a zone's rules change, floating time and other timescales such as TAI are not addressed.
sections.eli5: A plain timestamp says when, but not whose clock. This RFC adds an optional note at the end so programs can say more.

sections.title: Time Zones and Offsets
sections.content:
The RFC is careful about vocabulary. A UTC offset is the difference between local time and UTC, such as -05:00 for New York in the winter of 2023. A time zone is a set of rules mapping timestamps to offsets. It can also derive new timestamps from differences in local time. To compute 'one day later' in San Francisco, a zone is needed, because the local offset can change from one day to the next.

An IANA Time Zone is a named zone in the Time Zone Database, such as Europe/Paris or Asia/Tokyo. Using a named zone means the intent is that the rules current at the time of interpretation apply, even if they change later.

An offset time zone uses a numeric offset as the zone name, for example 2022-07-08T00:14:07+08:45[+08:45]. It is supported for backwards compatibility but strongly discouraged. Programs MUST NOT copy the offset from a timestamp into an offset time zone just to satisfy a program that wants a zone suffix, because that wrongly asserts the offset will never change. The RFC shows that adding six months to 2020-01-01T00:00+01:00[Europe/Paris] adjusts for summer time, while the same calculation with [+01:00] is off by one hour.
sections.eli5: An offset is just 'my clock is this many hours from the world clock'. A time zone is a whole rulebook, including when clocks jump forward for summer.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 3339 for the Offset Z
sections.content:
Section 4.3 of RFC 3339 said that an offset of Z or +00:00 implies that UTC is the preferred reference point for the time, and that -00:00 means the time in UTC is known but the offset to local time is not. That convention mirrored one in email headers, but ISO 8601 from the 2000 edition onward does not allow -00:00. Implementations that needed this meaning therefore tended to use Z.

RFC 9557 updates RFC 3339 to match practice. Section 4.3 is revised so that Z means the time in UTC is known but the offset to local time is unknown. This differs from +00:00, which still implies that UTC is the preferred reference point.

The RFC adds notes: the meaning of +00:00 is not changed, and -00:00 is not formally deprecated, but Z should now be used in its place.

This is why 2022-07-08T00:14:07Z[Europe/Paris] is not inconsistent. The Z does not claim any particular local zone, so the suffix can supply it.
sections.eli5: A Z used to mean 'world clock is my favorite'. Now it means 'I know the world-clock time, but I am not saying what my local clock showed'.

sections.title: The IXDTF Syntax
sections.content:
An IXDTF string is an RFC 3339 date-time followed by a suffix. The suffix is an optional time zone tag and any number of further tags. The grammar is given in ABNF as date-time-ext = date-time suffix.

A time zone tag is a name or numeric offset in square brackets, such as [America/Los_Angeles]. Other tags have a key and a value separated by an equals sign, such as [u-ca=hebrew]. Keys are lowercase only. A value can have several items separated by hyphens and is case-sensitive unless otherwise specified. A time zone tag is the one tag without an equals sign.

The RFC's examples all describe the same instant: 1996-12-19T16:39:57-08:00, the same with [America/Los_Angeles] added, and the same with [u-ca=hebrew] as well. A time zone name is intended to be an IANA Time Zone name. Because sender and receiver may use different revisions of the Time Zone Database, a recipient may not know a name and should treat that like any other inconsistency.

The grammar is deliberately permissive about the length of each zone name part. At the time of writing, the rules for naming limit each part to a maximum of 14 characters, but the local database controls the real limit.
sections.eli5: You write the usual timestamp, then add tags in square brackets, like stickers on a parcel: one saying which city's time, another saying which calendar to use.

sections.title: Elective and Critical Tags, and Inconsistencies
sections.content:
Suffix tags are always optional for the generator. By default they are also elective: the recipient may ignore any tag, for example because it does not know the key or cannot act on the value. A tag is critical when an exclamation mark follows its opening bracket. A recipient MUST NOT act on the string unless it can process a critical tag as specified.

A timestamp can be inconsistent with its zone tag. The RFC's example is 2022-07-08T00:14:07+01:00[Europe/Paris], because Europe/Paris did not use +01:00 in July 2022. With an elective tag, the recipient may treat the string as plain 2022-07-08T00:14:07+01:00. Inconsistency can arise from political decisions, from sender and receiver using different zone-database versions, or from program errors.

Rules for acting on an inconsistency:

  • If the time zone tag is critical, an application MUST act on the inconsistency, for example by rejecting the string or asking the user.
  • If it is not critical, the application MAY act on it.
  • An unrecognized critical tag, or a conflicting critical tag, makes the string erroneous.
  • If an elective key is duplicated and the application does no extra processing, it MUST choose the first suffix with that key.

Using Z avoids inconsistency: 2022-07-08T00:14:07Z[Europe/London] asserts no local offset, so the receiver works out the local time from the zone rules.
sections.eli5: A sticker can say 'nice to know' or 'you must read this' (the exclamation mark). If you cannot follow a must-read sticker, you should stop and ask instead of guessing.

sections.title: Tag Keys, Calendars and the Registry
sections.content:
The suffix key u-ca is allocated to indicate the calendar in which the date and time is preferably presented. Its values are those of the Unicode Calendar Identifier, such as hebrew in the RFC's example. It only suggests how to show a time, and the instant itself does not change.

IANA has created the registry "Timestamp Suffix Tag Keys" in a new group "Internet Date/Time Format". Each entry has a key identifier, a registration status of Provisional or Permanent, a description, a change controller and a reference. The initial content is u-ca. The policy is Specification Required for permanent entries and Expert Review for provisional ones, and the experts are told to be frugal with short, generic-sounding keys.

Keys that start with an underscore, such as _foo, are for experiments in controlled environments. They cannot be registered, MUST NOT be used for interchange, and MUST be rejected by implementations not configured for that experiment.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of sticker names. Names starting with an underscore are for private tests and must never be sent out into the world.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC raises three concerns. First, extra information can mean excessive disclosure. Revealing a calendar or language choice may tell recipients more about the sender than data minimization would allow, so generators should consider whether each piece is appropriate for all recipients and err on the side of minimizing it.

Second, extending any data format can create new vulnerabilities in parsers, but the RFC says no considerations are known for the IXDTF syntax that are out of the ordinary.

Third, parts of an IXDTF string may be inconsistent, now or with future extensions. Where actors must interpret data consistently for security, such as timestamps embedded in access control information, only extensions with a well-understood and shared way to resolve inconsistency can be used.
sections.eli5: Every note you add tells people something about you. Only add notes you are happy for the reader to know.
